questions.title: Can a defendant's deceptive conduct (using fake identities to solicit content) ever negate the 'good faith' requirement for fair use?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the court's handling of the 'bad faith' argument. Santos argued that Kimmel's use of fictitious names to trick him into making the videos constituted bad faith, citing *Harper & Row* which states fair use 'presupposes good faith.' However, the Second Circuit seemed to dismiss this by saying *Harper & Row*'s language on good faith has been 'distanced' by later cases and that the subjective intent doesn't matter. Does this mean that even egregious deception in obtaining the underlying work is irrelevant if the subsequent use is transformative? Or is there still a threshold where bad faith can kill a fair use defense regardless of transformativeness?

questions.title: How does the court distinguish between 'market substitution' and 'devaluation via parody' in the fourth fair use factor?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that for the fourth factor, we look at whether the second work usurps the market by being a competing substitute, not whether it damages the market by devaluing the original through criticism. The court notes that creators won't typically license parodies anyway. But isn't there a risk here? If Kimmel's segment effectively destroys Santos's ability to sell these specific types of inspirational videos because people now associate them with mockery rather than sincerity, wouldn't that be market harm? How exactly does the court draw the line between legitimate criticism that hurts sales (which is allowed) and a derivative market usurpation (which isn't) in this specific context?

questions.title: At what point does 'transformative use' become apparent enough to justify dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed dismissal at the pleading stage based on fair use. Usually, fair use involves factual disputes about how much was used or what the effect on the market is. Here, the court relied heavily on taking judicial notice of copyright registrations and looking at the complaint itself. What is the standard for deciding that a fair use defense is 'so clearly established' that no discovery is needed? Specifically, how did they determine that a reasonable observer would view Kimmel's purpose as commentary without needing evidence beyond what Santos himself alleged in his complaint?

questions.title: Does preemption analysis require resolving whether state contract claims are qualitatively different from copyright claims before dismissing for failure to state a claim?
questions.question_body: Regarding Santos's breach of contract and implied contract claims, I'm stuck on why the court didn't actually decide if these were preempted by Section 301 of the Copyright Act. The district court dismissed them on preemption grounds, but Santos appealed arguing they were qualitatively different. The appellate court said they 'need not resolve this issue' because the claims failed under state law anyway. Is it procedurally correct to skip over a major federal preemption question entirely just because there's an independent state-law reason for dismissal? Shouldn't preemption be addressed first since it goes to federal jurisdiction/authority?

questions.title: What constitutes sufficient pleading of an implied-in-fact contract regarding third-party terms of service under NY law?
questions.question_body: I don't understand why Santos couldn't rely on Kimmel breaching Cameo's Terms of Service (ToS). The court says Santos wasn't a party to ToS and Illinois law presumes against third-party beneficiaries unless explicitly declared. Then it switches to NY law for implied contracts but says Santos failed to plead essential terms or a 'meeting of minds.' Since Kimmel clicked 'agree' to ToS which included rules about not misrepresenting identity or using content commercially outside agreed scope, isn't that an objective manifestation of assent? Why does NY law require more than just one party adhering to known public terms when interacting with another person who relies on those terms?

questions.title: Is out-of-pocket loss strictly required for fraudulent inducement in New York when no direct financial transaction occurred?
questions.question_body: The fraudulent inducement claim was dismissed because Santos allegedly lacked 'out-of-pocket loss.' Santos made free videos; he didn't pay money to Kimmel directly (Kimmel paid Cameo). So where is his pecuniary loss? My confusion stems from whether providing labor/content in exchange for exposure/promotion counts as an investment where losing it due to fraud creates recoverable damages. If he spent time creating high-quality videos expecting genuine promotion but got mocked instead, shouldn't that lost opportunity cost or wasted effort count as an economic injury under *Lama Holding Co.* standards?
